The finding that stuck: most have adopted AI tools. Most haven't changed how they build software.

If you're thinking about where cloud agents fit into your engineering org, this is the conversation to be in.

The result:

recent_posts.title:
The biggest mistake engineering leaders are making with AI is treating codegen as the whole transformation.

Engineers only spend ~16% of their time actually writing code.

So even "perfect" AI codegen only attacks 16% of the system.

The real leverage is in context, workflows, review, docs, architecture, and removing bottlenecks.
recent_posts.summary: Engineering leaders are misallocating AI investment by focusing solely on code generation, which only addresses ~16% of engineers' actual time. The real productivity gains come from applying AI to context management, workflows, code review, documentation, architecture decisions, and bottleneck removal.

recent_posts.title:
In our testing, Opus 4.7 is noticeably better at staying on plan over longer horizons. It adapts when constraints change and follows through with verification instead of restarting mid-run.

It also reasons more deeply before acting, which shows up as more stable execution in async and automated workflows.

The difference we’ve seen:

- fewer tool-state failures
- fewer “re-derive the approach” turns
- stronger performance in CI/CD and long-running tasks
recent_posts.summary: Claude Opus 4.7 shows improved performance in long-horizon agentic tasks, with better plan adherence, deeper reasoning before acting, fewer tool-state failures, and stronger execution in CI/CD and automated workflows compared to previous versions.
